sn35.103:1.1: Uddaka was the second Brahmanical sage under whom the Bodhisatta practiced before awakening ([mn26:16.1]()). Another of his enigmatic sayings is found at [dn29:16.8](). When the Bodhisatta began his study, he first learned to recite the scriptures, and in these two passages we find examples of what those scriptures were. While none of Uddaka’s teachings have been found in the Vedic corpus, chapter 23 of the Jain Isibhāsiyāiṁ—a collection of sayings of various sages, including Buddhists and Vedists—is attributed to a certain Rāmaputta, who is likely the same person.
sn35.103:1.2: There seems no reason to doubt this is a genuine quote, but I have not been able to trace it as such. It seems to be a verse, albeit unmetrical. For the use of repeated initial pronouns in Vedic verse, see eg. Rig Veda 6.65.4–5. | The initial _idaṁ_ (neuter) serves as an emphatic particle disconnected from the nouns (masculine). It is an idiom of the Śatapatha Brāhmaṇa (eg. 3.6.1.5, 3.7.1.2, 3.8.2.15), where it serves to highlight a dramatic statement or gesture. In particular, in the opening passages it announces a transformed or realized self-identity (1.1.1.4: “Hereupon I enter from untruth to truth!”; 1.1.1.6: “Hereupon I become he who I am”). | A similar phrasing is employed by Brahmā Sahampati at [sn6.13:5.1](), where it emphasizes direct experience. | In early Sanskrit and Pali, _jātu_ usually has the sense “ever” or the emphatic “absolutely” (here, commentary glosses _ekaṁsena_; see too Śatapatha Brāhmaṇa 2.2.2.20, 14.6.8.1). | _Vedagū_ is not attested in Brahmanical texts, but it is perhaps a contraction of Sanskrit _vedapāraga_ in the same sense: “one versed in the Vedas”, such as Yājñavalkya (Mahābhārata 1.113.40). Given that in Buddhist literature it is assumed to be a term of the brahmins, perhaps the Buddha learned it under Uddaka from this very line.
sn35.103:1.4: The terms “dug” (_palikhata_ = Ardhamāgadhī _paḍighāta_) and “boil” (_gaṇḍa_), neither of which are particularly common, occur multiple times in Isibhāsiyāiṁ 23. It is remarkable that, although so few of Uddaka’s teachings are preserved, they share this striking language. Probably these were terms used by Uddaka himself; perhaps “boil”, like “knowledge master”, was adapted by the Buddha from this passage.
sn35.103:1.6: The Buddha makes explicit Uddaka’s saying as a claim to attainment. Isibhāsiyāiṁ 23 has rather a different tenor, as there Uddaka is depicted as lamenting the presence of the boils etc., and determining to practice “knowledge, vision, and good conduct” to bring an end to the beginningless course of transmigration. The story of the Bodhisatta’s studentship implies that Uddaka knew he was yet to attain the highest meditation that he taught ([mn26:16.9](), etc.).
sn35.103:4.2: Also at [an9.15:2.1](). Elsewhere, “boil” is a term for sensual pleasures ([an6.23]()) or for suffering ([sn22.122:1.4]()).
